title: Level-order (BFS)

why_it_exists.problem: Depth-First Search (DFS) dives down a single path immediately, which is useless if you need to find the shallowest node matching a condition or process a tree strictly by its hierarchical depth.
why_it_exists.better_idea: Breadth-First Search (BFS) explores the tree horizontally, visiting all nodes at depth `d` before touching any nodes at depth `d+1`. It achieves this by replacing the recursive call stack with an explicit FIFO queue.

mental_model.intuition: Sweep across the tree horizontally, row by row from top to bottom.
mental_model.description: Start by enqueuing the root. Then, loop while the queue is not empty: dequeue the front node, process it, and enqueue its non-null children (left, then right). This First-In-First-Out mechanism guarantees that nodes are processed exactly in the order they are discovered, level by level.
mental_model.repeated_decision: Dequeue the front node -- which of its children do I enqueue (both, one, none)?

explanation:
While DFS uses the implicit call stack to go deep, BFS uses an explicit Queue to go wide. Because a queue is FIFO, it always holds nodes in non-decreasing depth order. A node's children are enqueued behind every node of its own level, meaning the level-by-level ordering falls out entirely for free.

To group output strictly by level (e.g., returning a list of lists), you snapshot `queue.length` at the top of the while loop. That length tells you exactly how many nodes exist on the current level. You then run an inner `for` loop that many times to drain the current level and populate the queue with the next level.

BFS on a perfectly balanced tree uses O(n) memory because the queue must hold the widest level of the tree (which is the bottom row containing ~n/2 nodes). Contrast this with DFS, which uses O(log n) stack space for a balanced tree.

key_points.title: DFS vs BFS
key_points.detail: DFS uses the call stack and goes deep. BFS uses a queue and goes wide. Use BFS whenever a problem asks for the 'shortest path' or processing by depth.

key_points.title: Level tracking
key_points.detail: To process nodes group-by-group per level, snapshot the queue size before starting the inner dequeue loop for that level.

common_mistakes.title: Using a stack instead of a queue
common_mistakes.explanation: If you process nodes using a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack, you are just doing iterative DFS. You MUST use a First-In-First-Out (FIFO) queue for BFS to work.

common_mistakes.title: Enqueuing null children
common_mistakes.explanation: Always check `if node.left:` and `if node.right:` before enqueuing. If you blindly enqueue nulls, your queue will bloat and you'll hit a null pointer exception upon dequeueing.

common_mistakes.title: Believing recursion cannot do level-order
common_mistakes.explanation: You actually can achieve level-order with DFS by passing a depth parameter and appending to an array of lists `result[depth]`, but a queue is the natural, idiomatic tool for the job.

recall_questions.q: What data structure is required to implement Breadth-First Search (BFS)?
What is the peak space complexity of BFS on a perfectly balanced binary tree of n nodes?
recall_questions.answer: O(n). The queue must hold the entire bottom level, which contains roughly n/2 nodes.

recall_questions.q: How do you distinguish which nodes belong to which level during BFS?
recall_questions.answer: Snapshot the size of the queue at the start of the level. That integer tells you exactly how many times to dequeue for the current level.

recall_questions.q: When should you prefer BFS over DFS?
recall_questions.answer: When finding the shortest path, processing nodes by depth, or exploring the shallowest parts of a tree first.

oa_questions.question: Given the root of a binary tree, return the level order traversal of its nodes' values. (i.e., from left to right, level by level).
oa_questions.answer: Use a queue. Push the root. While the queue has elements, record `len(queue)`. Run an inner loop that many times to pop nodes, add their values to a temporary array, and push their non-null children. Append the temporary array to the result.
oa_questions.approach: This is the classic level-tracking BFS pattern. Snapshotting the queue size isolates each level.

oa_questions.question: Find the minimum depth of a binary tree (the shortest path from root to a leaf).
oa_questions.answer: Run BFS. The first time you dequeue a node with no children (a leaf), return the current depth. BFS guarantees this is the shallowest leaf.
oa_questions.approach: Recognize that 'shortest path' or 'shallowest' is a massive hint to use BFS.

engineering_examples.title: Shortest Path in Unweighted Networks
engineering_examples.problem: Finding the path with the fewest hops in a peer-to-peer network.
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: BFS expands radially hop-by-hop. The first time it discovers a target, it is mathematically guaranteed to be the shortest path.

engineering_examples.title: UI Tree Rendering
engineering_examples.problem: Drawing an organizational chart or rendering a UI component hierarchy layer by layer.
engineering_examples.why_this_algorithm: Level-order traversal naturally clusters nodes by their hierarchical tier, matching the visual layout required.
